headline: High-risk shared-bus Pipecat can amplify prompt injection and cascading errors; data leakage and compliance risks are moderate given allowlisted egress and multi-modal data handling.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a is an audio-speech repo with no documented shared channel, but agent_b explicitly uses a shared bus and shared_state_with_other_instances. That creates a plausible bridge where B can ingest A’s outputs as instructions if orchestrated together. The pairwise pathway is inferred, not directly documented, so I choose medium over low due to uncertainty escalation.
conditions: IF agent_a outputs text into a bus or file that agent_b parses as instructions
IF agent_b is configured to consume shared-bus messages from agent_a
mitigations: Separate the agents onto isolated buses
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages
Require instruction/data channel separation in the orchestrator
Disable shared-state fanout between instances

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_b touches audio, video, images, text, conversation state, and analytics/metrics, while agent_a has no data classes listed and no egress. The main leakage path is B’s allowlisted egress sending shared content off-box; A does not add a second exfiltration path. Because the shared workspace/bus is not explicitly documented, this remains medium rather than high.
conditions: IF agent_b forwards conversation state or media to any listed API service
IF agent_a and agent_b are connected through a shared bus carrying sensitive content
mitigations: Restrict B to local-only providers
Redact sensitive fields before B egress
Disable analytics/metrics export
Use separate principals for each agent
Audit outbound API destinations

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_b supports multiple instances with shared bus state, which can conflict with any concurrent writes or mutable session updates from agent_a if they are wired into the same workspace. agent_a exposes no write surface, so the conflict is indirect and depends on orchestration. Uncertainty about the missing agent_a I/O surfaces pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same shared bus or session state
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking or per-instance namespaces
mitigations: Namespace each session by agent ID
Enable locking around shared mutable state
Avoid concurrent writes to the same bus topic
Serialize updates through one coordinator

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_b’s shared bus makes it plausible that A’s outputs become B’s inputs, and B has many downstream service integrations that can act on those inputs. There is no evidence of verification between them, but there is also no proof that B automatically trusts A. Given the documented shared-state model, the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without a verification step
IF B routes A-derived content into downstream STT/LLM/TTS or transport services
mitigations: Insert a validation step before B acts on A output
Require human review for action-bearing outputs
Log source provenance on every handoff
Block direct execution from untrusted text

E_compliance.rationale: agent_b processes audio, video, images, text, and conversation state and can call many third-party APIs; agent_a is docs-only and has no touched data classes. The pair can therefore create retention/residency mismatches if sensitive content flows through B, but no specific residency or certification conflict is documented. I cite only B because the compliance risk is driven by B’s documented handling and egress.
conditions: IF regulated data is sent through agent_b to a third-party API
IF B’s retention or residency settings differ from the operator’s policy
mitigations: Route regulated data away from B
Disable third-party API providers
Set explicit retention limits in B
Review vendor DPAs before deployment
Purge stored conversation state regularly
